title: Words at Crow Agency
description: A source-based historical adventure about translation, authority, and the record left behind after a crisis.
learningObjectives: Describe what happened at the Crow Agency during the Sword Bearer incident of 1887.
Explain the positions of Crow leaders, the agent, and the army.
Evaluate how the incident was reported by the people involved.

player.name: Agency Interpreter
player.brief: You translate between officials, soldiers, and Crow leaders. Your words cannot stop every event, but they can shape what each side hears and what later gets recorded.

sharedContext.text: You serve as an interpreter at Crow Agency. After a raid on the Piegans, gunfire at the Agency has led Henry Williamson to call in troops from Fort Custer. Over the next weeks, you will hear how the agent, Crow leaders, and the army describe the same crisis, and you will help decide what gets said clearly, softened, or left out.

assumptions.text: The player is an interpreter working at Crow Agency during the crisis.
assumptions.rationale: The teacher brief sets the student role, but the sources do not identify a specific interpreter-player.

assumptions.text: Stage 1 uses an office, street, and yard inside the Agency as playable spaces.
assumptions.rationale: The sources mention the Agency and its buildings, but not a room-by-room layout.

assumptions.text: Stage 2 uses a parley yard, command tent, and open field near the Agency.
assumptions.rationale: The sources describe meetings, troops, and fighting, but not exact spatial arrangement.

assumptions.text: Stage 3 uses a council chamber, records office, and yard for the December meeting.
assumptions.rationale: The council minutes confirm a meeting at the Agency, but not the specific rooms.

assumptions.text: The player can soften Williamson's message by stressing protection before arrests.
assumptions.rationale: The exact wording of any interpreter in this moment is not preserved.

assumptions.text: If the player refuses to carry Williamson's message, the player is removed from the process.
assumptions.rationale: This is a counterfactual branch needed for gameplay; the sources do not record it.

assumptions.text: Plenty Coos is present during the November standoff as a leading Crow voice.
assumptions.rationale: The sources name him in the December council, not in the failed November peace meeting.

assumptions.text: The player can press for one more distinct parley between elders and soldiers before shooting starts.
assumptions.rationale: The sources say a meeting failed, but they do not preserve every possible exchange.

assumptions.text: The player may step back from active mediation and focus on observing and recording.
assumptions.rationale: This creates a plausible interpretive stance not specified in the documents.

assumptions.text: A harsher translation can narrow the space for mediation and end the player's role early.
assumptions.rationale: This is a counterfactual gameplay branch rather than a documented event.

assumptions.text: The player helps shape the written emphasis of the December council minutes.
assumptions.rationale: The minutes note an interpreter was present, but they do not identify that person's choices in wording or emphasis.

assumptions.text: Light snow is used as an atmospheric overlay for late December at Crow Agency.
assumptions.rationale: The date is known, but the weather on that day is not given in the sources.

assumptions.text: Williamson privately wants to show Washington that he still controls the Agency.
assumptions.rationale: His letter shows urgency and a demand for arrests, but not an explicit confession of motive.

assumptions.text: Dudley privately wants to protect the Agency without exceeding orders and inviting blame.
assumptions.rationale: The letter reports prompt action and limited instructions, but not his inner reasoning.

assumptions.text: Plenty Coos privately tries to separate the wider Crow community from Sword Bearer's band while bringing prisoners home.
assumptions.rationale: His later council remarks support prisoner return and orderly relations, but do not state this exact strategy.

assumptions.text: Sword Bearer believes armed defiance can win status and followers among young men.
assumptions.rationale: The sources describe him as a Messianic leader and note defiance, but not his private thoughts.

Williamson then turns the discussion to whether Mr. Cummins and his family should be adopted as Crows. Your task is no longer battlefield language. It is historical emphasis.

endings.title: Removed from the Conversation
endings.summary: You refuse to carry the agent's preferred message. Another interpreter or clerk is found, and the crisis moves on without your voice in it.

endings.divergence: This branch departs from the record by removing you from the process before the November and December stages.
reflectionQuestions: What power does an interpreter have if they refuse to speak at all?
Does stepping away prevent harm, or does it simply give the loudest voices more control?
How does this branch change what later historians would know?

endings.title: The Line Hardens
endings.summary: Your uncompromising message closes the space for mediation. Fighting comes before any fuller record can include your doubts.

historicalOutcome.text: The documents say that after peace failed, 'a fight broke out between Companies E and K of the 1st Cavalry and about 150 Crows.' In the end, 'the Crows retreated, and Sword Bearer was killed.'

endings.divergence: This branch makes your wording part of the immediate escalation and ends your role before the later council record.
reflectionQuestions: When does 'clear language' become a tool of escalation?
How much responsibility belongs to the interpreter, and how much to the people giving orders?
Why might official reports still describe the violence as necessary?

endings.title: The Minutes Stand
endings.summary: You preserve the council in the order it survives: the plea for the prisoners is heard, but the written discussion moves on to adoption and consent.

historicalOutcome.text: At the December council, Plenty Coos asked that the 'eight Crow prisoners now held at' Fort Snelling 'come home to us pretty' quick. The Agent then replied that some desired 'to adopt Mr. Cummins.' The surviving minutes preserve both the prison request and the shift of subject.

endings.divergence: This ending matches the source record most closely.
reflectionQuestions: Why might Williamson move from prisoners to adoption?
What does the order of topics do to the meaning of the council?
How should historians read a source that may be accurate in wording but selective in emphasis?

endings.title: A Different Emphasis
endings.summary: You force the written appeal to center the prisoners and the labor their families have lost. The meeting still discusses adoption, but not before the prison question is made impossible to ignore.

historicalOutcome.text: In the actual record, the prisoners remained central to Plenty Coos, who asked that they return because they could help their families work, yet the minutes also went on to the unanimous adoption of the Cummins family.
